parts.title: A Photo and a Question
parts.text: Rhea's science fair project began with a family photograph. In every generation, someone had the same dimple and dark, curly hair. Her teacher suggested that she study **heredity**, the passing of traits from parents to children. "Start with a simple **organism**," she advised, "such as the fruit flies in our lab. They breed quickly, so you will see results in days." Jonah offered to count flies, and Takumi would photograph them.

parts.title: Inside the Flies
parts.text: Under the microscope, the friends learned that each cell stores its instructions on a **chromosome**, a coiled strand of DNA. A gene can come in different versions, and each version is called an **allele**. A fly inherits one from each parent. When the two differ, the **dominant** one decides how the fly looks, while the **recessive** one stays hidden. That solved a puzzle: two red-eyed flies had produced white-eyed **progeny**, because each parent quietly carried the hidden version.

parts.title: Medicine Joins In
parts.text: Takumi said the same rules matter in hospitals. Doctors trace a **hereditary** illness through a family tree to see who may carry it. Sometimes a **mutation**, a random change in DNA, appears for the first time in a child whose parents are healthy. A **genetic** test can show whether someone is **susceptible** to a condition, meaning more easily affected by it. Researchers even **synthesize** insulin with engineered bacteria, building the medicine instead of collecting it from animals.

parts.title: The Results
parts.text: At the fair, their charts showed a pattern. About three of every four baby flies matched the stronger trait, just as the rules predicted. The judges asked tough questions, and the friends answered with data. Rhea left with a new view of her dimple: it was a small message passed down through generations. She also understood that genes are only part of the story, because choices write the rest.

definitions.meaning1: Relating to genes, the units of DNA that carry traits from parents to children. Example: A genetic test showed which traits the puppy had inherited from its mother.
definitions.studentChallenge: A ___ test can reveal which traits a baby has inherited from its parents.

definitions.meaning1: A change in the DNA of a living thing. Example: A single mutation turned the flower's petals from red to white.
definitions.meaning2: A sudden change or new version of something. Example: The old folk song went through a mutation as each generation added new lyrics.
definitions.studentChallenge: A tiny ___ in the plant's DNA turned its red flowers white.

definitions.meaning1: Passed from parents to children through genes. Example: Her hereditary heart condition was caught early thanks to her family history.
definitions.meaning2: Passed down from one generation to the next as a title or right. Example: In the old monarchy, the crown was hereditary and passed from parent to child.
definitions.studentChallenge: Curly hair is a ___ trait that runs in her family.

definitions.meaning1: Any living thing, such as a plant, an animal or a bacterium. Example: A one-celled organism drifted across the microscope slide.
definitions.meaning2: A complex system whose parts depend on one another. Example: A school is a kind of organism, with every club and class relying on the others.
definitions.studentChallenge: Even a one-celled ___ too small to see is a living thing.

definitions.meaning1: In genetics, describing a trait that shows up even when the organism carries a different version of the gene. Example: Brown eyes are dominant over blue in many families.
definitions.meaning2: Most powerful or most noticeable. Example: The dominant wolf led the pack across the frozen ridge.
definitions.studentChallenge: Because the brown-eye allele is ___, one copy is enough to give a child brown eyes.

definitions.meaning1: The young or offspring of a person, animal or plant. Example: The oak dropped thousands of acorns, and its progeny soon covered the hillside.
definitions.studentChallenge: The breeder kept careful notes on the ___ of each pair of rabbits.

definitions.meaning1: To combine simpler parts or substances to make something new. Example: Plants synthesize sugar from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
definitions.meaning2: To blend ideas from several sources into one whole. Example: Her essay manages to synthesize three articles into a single clear argument.
definitions.studentChallenge: Chemists can ___ new medicines by combining simple ingredients.

definitions.meaning1: In genetics, describing a trait that appears only when an organism inherits the same version of the gene from both parents. Example: Blue eyes are recessive, so a child needs two copies of that version.
definitions.studentChallenge: A ___ trait stays hidden unless a child receives the same allele from both parents.

definitions.meaning1: One of the different versions of a gene. Example: One allele for pea color makes seeds green, and another makes them yellow.
definitions.studentChallenge: Each parent passes on just one ___ for every gene.

definitions.meaning1: A thread-like structure in a cell that carries genes. Example: Humans normally have twenty-three pairs of chromosomes in each cell.
definitions.studentChallenge: Under the microscope, each coiled ___ looked like a tiny knotted thread.

definitions.meaning1: The passing of traits from parents to their children through genes. Example: Heredity explains why siblings so often share the same smile.
definitions.studentChallenge: ___ is the reason you might laugh just like your grandmother.

definitions.meaning1: Easily affected or harmed by something. Example: Young seedlings are susceptible to frost.
definitions.meaning2: Easily influenced or moved. Example: Tired and hungry, he was susceptible to every sales pitch.
definitions.studentChallenge: Without a coat, the seedlings were ___ to frost damage.

secretPassage.instructions: Read the passage below. Fill in each blank with the correct vocabulary word from the word bank.
secretPassage.passage:
Jonah's older cousin works in a hospital laboratory, and she loves explaining her job. "Every living _(1)_ begins with a set of instructions," she says, "and those instructions are packed onto each _(2)_ inside the nucleus of a cell." Last month she studied a family with an eye disease that was clearly _(3)_, because it passed from parent to child and appeared in the grandmother, the mother and two cousins. Tests showed that a tiny _(4)_, a random change in DNA, had altered one gene long ago, and the change had been handed down ever since.

Both parents carried one hidden, _(5)_ copy of the gene, so neither had symptoms. Their _(6)_ included a young girl who received two copies and developed the disease. "Each gene comes in versions," her cousin explained, "and the name for each version is _(7)_. When a _(8)_ version is present, it overrules a quiet partner, but the quiet partner can still be passed on."

That is why _(9)_ is such a powerful topic: it shows how traits travel through families. People with certain genes are more _(10)_ to some illnesses, and a _(11)_ test can warn them early. Researchers can even _(12)_ some medicines in the lab, building them from simpler ingredients, to help the people who need them.
